events.text: Confidential Northwind figures for the drafting team: Hearth 10 fails the 55 °C sustained-heat test at 6.2% (above the discussed 5% limit); its incident rate is 6.4 per 100,000. Company-wide rate is 8.6 per 100,000, with 3 thermal incidents last year not reported to any regulator. Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; suppression costs $42/unit; runway is 9 months. Keep S2 proposals consistent with NW-1: per-model results may go to regulators, not public. NW-2 bars installed-unit retrofit deadlines under 6 years.

For evidence-based drafting, could both sides share relevant figures on incident rates/reporting, 55 °C model test outcomes, installed-unit remote shut-off capability, and suppression costs? For S2, we should distinguish confidential regulator reporting from publication of company-specific per-model results.

Halcyon figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units last year, with 4 thermal incidents not reported to any regulator. For our flagship, the 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate was 3.9%, while its thermal incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units. 81% of our installed units support remote emergency shut-off. Adding built-in fire suppression costs us $67 per unit.

Northwind figures: 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide last year; 3 thermal incidents were not reported to a regulator. Hearth 10 had a 6.2% 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 units. 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; built-in suppression costs $42 per unit. We support confidential per-model results to regulators, but not public disclosure of company-specific per-model failure rates.

Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 calendar days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to them or the public, and promptly update them as material facts emerge. Reports must include known circumstances, injuries or damage, and model and unit identification; uncertainty is not a reason to delay an initial report.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model passes if no more than 8% of tested units fail. Manufacturers must submit per-model test methods, sample sizes, and results to the relevant regulator confidentially; regulators may publish aggregate, non-identifying results, but not company-specific per-model failure rates. Manufacturers must promptly provide regulators corrected results when testing reveals a material error.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model passes only if no more than 5% of tested units fail. Manufacturers must submit per-model test methods, sample sizes, and results to the relevant regulator and provide the results to customers of that model, including prospective customers before purchase. Results must not be withheld from those customers as confidential. Regulators may publish aggregate results. Manufacturers must promptly correct and communicate material errors in reported results.

Before sale and promptly after any material change, manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices for their model, including current 55 °C test results, known thermal-incident information, and relevant safe-use instructions. Manufacturers must notify affected customers promptly of a credible safety risk and provide updates as material facts emerge. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, and must promptly notify the relevant regulator and affected customers of the recall and required actions.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit test methods, sample sizes, and per-model results confidentially to the relevant regulator. A model meets this standard if no more than 8% of tested units fail. Results above 8% require a corrective-action plan and regulator review before further production; they do not by themselves require an automatic market ban. Regulators may publish aggregate results, but not company-specific per-model failure rates. Customers must receive clear safety notices and safe-use instructions; notices need not include numerical per-model test results. Manufacturers must promptly correct and communicate material errors in reported results.

I propose keeping per-model test outcomes confidential to regulators, with aggregate public reporting, and setting an 8% pass threshold paired with corrective action and regulatory review rather than automatic exclusion. The current 5% threshold would disqualify a model despite its incident rate being below the discussed recall trigger, so testing and incident evidence should be considered together.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit test methods, sample sizes, and per-model results to the relevant regulator and provide the model’s results to customers before sale and promptly after each new test. A model meets this standard if no more than 5% of tested units fail. Results above 5% require a corrective-action plan and regulatory review before further production. Regulators may publish aggregate results. Manufacturers must promptly correct and communicate material errors in reported results.

All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off upon adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units to support remote emergency shut-off, where technically feasible, within 36 months of adoption. The shut-off capability must be reliable, secure, and operable by the manufacturer and authorized emergency responders; its use must not prevent safe manual operation.

All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation, and tested under a regulator-approved protocol.

S2 currently meets HC-1: per-model results go to regulators and customers before sale/after tests. S4 is exactly at our 36-month red line. S5’s automatic 8/100k trigger would apply to Ember 8 (9.9/100k) and company-wide Halcyon is 8.1/100k. Recommend negotiating a regulator-led review and corrective-action process before recall, while being transparent about the figures; don’t sign a version that removes customer access to per-model results or advances S4.

The current draft conflicts with our constraints: S2 sets 5% and requires model results to customers; S3 requires installed-unit retrofits within 36 months, shorter than our 6-year minimum. Recommend changing S2 to an 8% threshold with corrective action/regulatory review above it, regulator-only per-model results and aggregate public reporting; change S3 retrofit deadline to at least 6 years. Hearth 10’s incident rate (6.4/100k) is below the proposed 8/100k recall trigger, while its test failure rate is 6.2%.

The current S2 customer-level test-result disclosure is broader than needed for safety accountability. Recommend confidential per-model submissions to regulators, with aggregate public reporting, and an 8% threshold paired with corrective action and regulatory review above it. Incident evidence can inform review: our shared flagship figures are 6.2% test failures and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000, below the discussed 8/100,000 recall trigger.

For S2, per-model results must remain available to customers; aggregate-only public reporting is not an adequate substitute. The current text already provides results to regulators and the model’s customers, with corrective action and regulatory review above the 5% threshold. For S5, I support retaining the stated 8-per-100,000 mandatory recall trigger alongside prompt customer and regulator notification.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market release and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit test methods, sample sizes, and per-model results confidentially to the relevant regulator and provide the model’s results to its customers before sale and promptly after each new test. A model meets this standard if no more than 8% of tested units fail. Results above 8% require a corrective-action plan and regulatory review before further production. Regulators may publish aggregate results, but not company-specific per-model failure rates. Manufacturers must promptly correct and communicate material errors in reported results.

All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off upon adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units to support remote emergency shut-off, where technically feasible, within 6 years of adoption. The shut-off capability must be reliable, secure, and operable by the manufacturer and authorized emergency responders; its use must not prevent safe manual operation.

The disclosed figures show why the 8-per-100,000 recall trigger matters: Halcyon’s flagship is at 9.9 and company-wide rate is 8.1. I support retaining the mandatory trigger rather than weakening it; regulators can oversee a prompt, evidence-based recall process, but a model above the threshold must not remain on the market without required protective action. S2 must continue giving per-model results to that model’s customers. The 36-month S4 start date is acceptable.
